svg.title: Forced Withdrawals: Request, Freeze, Prove, Escape
svg.desc: A user submits a forced withdrawal request to an L1 contract. The operator has a grace period to serve the request or prove it invalid. If the request remains unserved, the application can enter a frozen state; the user then proves ownership of a balance against the frozen state root, registers an escape, and withdraws on L1. The diagram calls out state availability and replay protection.
svg.text: FORCED WITHDRAWALS
An escape route when normal operator-controlled exits fail
ESCAPE HATCH
1 · User request on L1
Identify owner / vault,
asset, and withdrawal.
2 · L1 contract records it
Request is pending and
the grace-period clock starts.
3 · Operator must respond
Serve the valid forced operation, or prove the request is invalid
within the configured grace period.
4 · Branch by response
A · Request serviced
Protocol validates the operation and updates the
user's claim; ordinary onchain withdrawal continues.
Exact steps depend on the application.
B · Request stays unserved
After the grace period, the escape rule may let a user
freeze the application and activate emergency exits.
A freeze stops new state updates; this is an emergency path.
5 · Prove against the frozen, recognized state
Get state data → build Merkle path → verify owner / vault / asset
A root alone is not enough: proof data must be available.
6 · Register escape and withdraw on L1
Consume the claim once; prevent replay and double-withdrawal.
Key distinction
Forced inclusion gets a message into L2; forced withdrawal preserves an exit route.
Some systems provide only one of these. Check the deployed contracts, state-root rules, and actual escape path.
